document.title: Post-Technical Conference Comments and Responses of The PJM Power Providers Group re PJM Governance and Stakeholder Reforms
document.group: PJM governance and stakeholder reform vote

pages.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
PJM Governance and Stakeholder Reforms 
) 
        Docket No. AD26-7-000 
POST-TECHNICAL CONFERENCE COMMENTS AND  
RESPONSES TO COMMISSION QUESTIONS OF  
THE PJM POWER PROVIDERS GROUP (P3) 
The PJM Power Providers Group ("P3") submits these post-technical conference comments in 
response to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission's ("Commission" or "FERC") July 30, 
2026, Notice Requesting Post-Conference Comments in Docket No. AD26-7-000. P3 is a non-
profit organization dedicated to promoting properly designed and well-functioning competitive 
markets in the PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. ("PJM") region. Combined, P3 members own and 
operate over 108,000 MWs of generation assets and produce enough power to supply over 63 
million homes across 13 states and the District of Columbia.1 
I. CORE GOVERNANCE PRINCIPLES 
•  Anchor All Reforms in Market Integrity & Merchant Capital Investibility: PJM's core 
mandate must remain operating robust, competitive wholesale markets that ensure reliability at the 
lowest reasonable cost. Governance reforms must not become a vehicle for compromising 
Regional Transmission Organization (“RTO”) independence or upending the stakeholder model. 
PJM's success hinges on attracting private merchant capital; reforms that introduce political 
volatility or regulatory uncertainty will damage investor confidence at a moment in time when 
investor confidence must be paramount. 
•  Uphold Section 205 Balance of Filing Rights: The division of Federal Power Act (“FPA”) 
Section 205 filing rights is a core structural feature of the PJM region. Suggestions to unilaterally 
broaden the PJM Board's or any state/stakeholder body's filing rights over matters traditionally 
 
1 The comments contained herein represent the position of P3 as an organization, but not necessarily the views of 
any particular member with respect to any issue.

reserved for Transmission Owners or the Members Committee risk destabilizing the careful 
balance struck in PJM. FPA Section 205 rights belong exclusively to jurisdictional service 
providers and cannot be involuntarily reallocated. 
•  Resist Expansion of Unilateral Board Authority: While the Board possesses necessary Tariff 
authority to act in true emergencies, unilateral action must remain an extraordinary tool. Routine 
expansion of unilateral Board authority erodes transparency, bypasses stakeholder expertise, and 
results in poorly formulated filings that burden the Commission and courts.  
•  Preserve Board Independence:  Having an independent Board that is accountable to the 
mandate of the PJM Operating Agreement is essential to the integrity of the PJM mission.  Where 
they are authorized to act, Board members should act in the best interest of the grid and the market 
after hearing input from PJM members and states.  PJM’s mission is defined in the Operating 
Agreement and that should be the standard by which the Board is evaluated. 
• 
Respect Core Mission vs. Political Priorities: PJM sits at the crossroads of 14 
jurisdictions with divergent policy goals. PJM's core mission is to reliably operate an interstate 
grid and dispatch lowest-cost resources via a competitive market. PJM must not be diverted from 
this mission and must remain focused on the market that serves state in the entire region. 
II. RESPONSES TO SPECIFIC QUESTIONS IN APPENDIX 
# 
Question / Theme 
P3 Position 
Detailed Explanation & Justification 
1 
Should Board members' terms 
be extended to five or more 
years? 
Yes 
P3 believes the current three-year term is 
too short and should be extended.   Five-
year terms seem appropriate. 
2 
Should there be a maximum 
number of years that a Board 
member may serve (e.g., 10 
years)? 
Neutral 
P3 does not have a strong view on term 
limits. 
3 
Should Board member 
qualification rules be revised 
to provide a preference for 
Yes 
P3 supports a preference, but not a 
requirement, that at least one board member 
resides in the PJM footprint.

some Board members that 
reside in the PJM region? 
4 
Should conflict-of-interest 
rules be revised to reduce the 
cooling off period for Board 
members from two years to 
one year? 
Yes 
P3 believes that a one year cooling off 
period is sufficient and will widen the pool 
of qualified candidates. 
5 
Should restrictions on Board 
communications be relaxed to 
enable more communication 
between the Board and 
stakeholders? 
Yes 
P3 appreciates the efforts that the Board has 
made in recent years to increase 
communications with stakeholders 
including the Liaison Committee and Board 
participation at the Members Committee 
meeting.  That said, any revised rules 
should not allow for preferential access by 
any particular constituency. 
6 
In order to increase 
transparency, should Board 
votes be made public or the 
Board be required to explain 
its reasoning? 
Yes 
Written explanations for major tariff or 
policy decisions enhance regulatory 
transparency, can provide crucial market 
clarity, and build confidence among market 
participants and investors.  P3 is not yet 
prepared to endorse disclosure of specific 
board member votes which could 
undermine Board independence. 
7 
In order to increase 
transparency, should some 
Board meetings be open or 
available to the public? 
Yes 
If done properly, opening non-confidential, 
strategic Board sessions to public 
observation fosters trust and alignment. 
Confidential executive sessions should 
remain for market sensitive rule changes, 
proprietary, personnel, or legal matters. 
8 
Should PJM's governing 
documents be revised to 
explicitly state that the 
responsibility of PJM and its 
No 
PJM's core mandate is to operate an 
interstate grid and robust competitive 
markets under the Federal Power Act. 
'Public interest' is an ambiguous, ill-defined 
standard in wholesale market governance

Board is to serve the public 
interest? 
that risks politicizing decisions and forcing 
PJM to balance conflicting state social 
policies rather than focusing on market 
efficiency and reliability. The PJM Board 
should not be responsible for determining 
what is in the “public interest” for the 13-
state PJM region.  Also, on August 19, the 
PJM members approved a change to the 
PJM Operating Agreement that makes clear 
that the PJM market should be designed and 
operated for the benefit of consumers. 
9 
Should state representatives 
have at least one voting 
member on the Nominating 
Committee? 
Potentially. 
P3 supports state participation in the 
Nominating Committee, however, given the 
unique nature of public officials 
participating in a very sensitive process, 
PJM members need to be comfortable that 
states can participate without undermining 
the integrity of the Nominating Committee 
process. P3 believes that the best path 
forward is to allow a state representative to 
observe and understand the Nominating 
Committee process before determining 
whether a state voting role is appropriate 
and desired by the states. 
10 
Should PJM adopt public 
performance metrics and tie 
management compensation to 
their achievement? 
No position. 
P3 does not understand what is meant by 
“public performance metrics,” but as a 
general matter feels that management 
compensation is a matter between the PJM 
Board and PJM management. 
11 
Should the stakeholder 
process be advisory, i.e., 
stakeholder votes only inform 
the Board? 
No 
Demoting the stakeholder process to purely 
advisory status would damage market 
participant engagement and investor 
confidence and is inconsistent with the 
governance balance struck in PJM as 
discussed above. Sector-weighted voting

provides critical commercial discipline and 
ensures well-vetted proposals reach FERC. 
12 
Should PJM have section 205 
filing rights over energy and 
ancillary services 
unencumbered by the 2/3 
Members Committee 
approval? 
No 
FPA Section 205 filing rights belong 
strictly to jurisdictional entities providing 
market services. Unilaterally granting PJM 
unencumbered filing rights over 
energy/ancillary services upsets the balance 
and bypasses essential stakeholder review.   
13 
Should PJM have section 205 
filing rights over Regional 
Transmission Expansion 
Planning (RTEP) 
unencumbered by 2/3 
Members Committee 
approval? 
No 
Transmission planning involves massive 
capital allocations and cost shifts across 
states and market participants. Retaining 
required stakeholder oversight and 
protecting Transmission Owners' statutory 
rights prevents unvetted, costly expansion 
mandates. 
14 
Should OPSI have 'jump ball' 
rights over resource adequacy 
and transmission cost 
allocation filings when a 
supermajority of OPSI agrees? 
No 
Granting 'jump ball' filing rights to state 
regulators violates Section 205 of the FPA, 
which reserves filing rights exclusively to 
jurisdictional public utilities. Litigating this 
question is in no one’s best interest so it 
should not be pursued. 
15 
Should the Members 
Committee have 'jump ball' 
filing rights over portions of 
the tariff where PJM has 205 
rights when a supermajority 
approves an alternative? 
No 
See comments above.  The current 
allocation of 205 rights in PJM is consistent 
with the Federal Power Act and the 
introduction of “jump ball” rights in any 
form introduces legal questions that are best 
avoided. 
16 
Should the approval threshold 
in the Members Committee be 
lowered from two-thirds 
sector-weighted voting? 
No 
The two-thirds sector-weighted voting 
threshold forces broad cross-sector 
consensus, preventing any single sector or 
coalition from imposing harmful rules on 
others.

17 
Should the voting rules 
barring affiliate votes, which 
apply to senior standing 
committees, also apply to 
lower-level committees? 
No position 
P3 members have differing views on 
affiliate voting in lower-level committees. 
18 
In addition to OPSI, should 
there be a second state 
representative group 
consisting of governors' 
representatives and/or state 
legislators? 
No 
Creating a second state body would 
duplicate efforts, confuse the stakeholder 
process, and further politicize technical 
market discussions. OPSI already serves as 
the recognized, effective liaison for state 
regulatory interests.  P3 prefers that the 
PJM governors and commissioners unify 
under a single organization – which is our 
understanding of what is happening. 
19 
Should state representatives 
have a formal voting role in 
the stakeholder process 
(limited to certain topics) in 
addition to consumer advocate 
votes? 
No 
State utility commissions act as regulators, 
not jurisdictional wholesale market 
participants. Giving states direct voting 
rights creates potential conflicts of interest. 
Moreover, it is our understanding that states 
do not want voting rights in the Stakeholder 
process. 
20 
Should PJM be required to 
consult with OPSI prior to 
making a section 205 filing 
related to resource adequacy 
and transmission cost 
allocation? 
Yes 
Consultation with state regulators via OPSI 
on critical resource adequacy and cost 
allocation matters is standard practice and 
enhances proposal durability. However, 
consultation must not amount to a state veto 
or delay urgent filings which would 
undermine PJM independence. Nothing in 
the current rules prevents this consultation 
from occurring now.

III.  COMMENTS 
The governance reforms under consideration in this proceeding cannot be evaluated in a vacuum. 
PJM stands at a critical juncture in its history, defined by unprecedented demand expansion and a 
generational transformation of the power fleet. Driven by the explosive growth of data centers and 
widespread electrification, electricity demand across the 13-state and District of Columbia 
footprint is growing at rates never seen. 
At the same time, power developers are stepping up to meet this moment with extraordinary 
commercial interest. Today, over 55 GW of new generation capacity has already cleared PJM’s 
interconnection queue and stands ready for construction, while PJM's recent interconnection queue 
Cycle 1 saw a record-shattering wave of project applications totaling over 220 GW.2 Furthermore, 
PJM’s request for information for generation developers interested in serving large loads drew 
over 130 GW of developer proposals eager to contract directly with new energy-intensive 
customers.3 
The overwhelming regulatory mandate facing PJM and the Commission is clear: the region must 
turn its immediate, undivided focus toward executing contracts for new supply, establishing 
clear federal and state rules related to the integration of large loads, expanding transmission 
capacity, and delivering power reliably to the grid. Meeting this challenge will require billions 
of dollars in private, at-risk merchant capital and it is axiomatic that investor capital flows where 
regulatory and market rules are predictable, stable, and transparent. 
Distracting PJM, state regulators, and market participants with prolonged structural governance 
debates—or worse, adopting governance changes that politicize PJM Board decisions, dilute 
sector-weighted voting, or destabilize FPA Section 205 filing rights—risks fracturing investor 
confidence at the exact moment it is needed most. PJM’s existing market structure and stakeholder 
 
2 PJM recently announced that 200 GWs advanced to the next step and are qualified to be studied.   See, 
https://insidelines.pjm.com/over-700-new-generation-projects-accepted-into-first-cycle-of-reformed-
interconnection-process/ 
 
3 See, https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/committees-groups/cifp-rbp/2026/20260527/20260527-informational-
only---reliability-backstop-rfi-summary---charles-river-associates.pdf.

model have proven their resilience through prior energy transitions.  Recent challenges are more 
reflective of decisions within the governance structure, which includes a large role for the 
Commission, rather than a flaw in the governance structure itself. Rather than upending a 
governance framework that largely works despite some imperfections, the Commission and PJM 
should maintain market integrity, preserve core negotiated and statutory balances, and stay focused 
on the monumental work of ensuring grid reliability and market efficiency for the millions of 
consumers PJM serves. 
IV.  CONCLUSION 
WHEREFORE, for the foregoing reasons, P3 respectfully requests that the Commission take 
these comments and responses to the Commission’s specific questions under consideration in 
taking any further action with respect to PJM’s governance and stakeholder processes. 
 
Respectfully submitted, 
 
The PJM Power Providers Group
